editorial.headline: A One-Star Hotel, With Bali’s Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This short-stay hotel activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a Bali PMA registration turns on the scope and OSS risk classification declared.
editorial.body:
One-star hotels are a deceptively specific accommodation business. This activity covers short-stay accommodation, generally offered daily or weekly, that meets one-star hotel requirements and uses part or all of a building. It expressly includes buildings of up to 6,000 square metres and those above that size. Rooms and suites may be furnished, while the operating model remains recognisably hotel-led: direct customer service on site, with possible daily cleaning and bed-making, food and beverage service, laundry, and conference or convention facilities. The business is not simply providing a room; it is providing serviced, short-term hotel accommodation.

Registration is open to small, medium and large businesses. That range gives the activity room to operate at different scales without changing its essential identity: a one-star hotel serving short-stay guests directly. The two building-size bands reinforce the point. The scope is not confined to a single physical footprint, but it does remain tied to accommodation that qualifies as a one-star hotel.

At the national level, foreign investment is permitted in this activity up to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is the national position, but it does not settle every local registration outcome. Bali applies a more exacting distinction. The Bali record does not categorically block PMA registration for this activity; instead, the outcome depends on the scope declared. At the large-business scale, some scopes carry low OSS risk while others carry a higher risk. PMA registration in Bali is available only when the higher-risk scope is declared, and the exact activity should be verified live in OSS.

That qualification is substantive. Bali’s permanent, province-wide moratorium blocks all activities classified as low or medium-low risk from PMA. The national 100% ceiling therefore does not automatically produce a Bali registration route. A founder considering Bali must read the activity through the precise scope and risk classification declared in OSS: this hotel activity can be registrable for PMA there, but only on the higher-risk side of that classification. That is the real line between a national opening and a Bali filing.
